t: Introduction: what forensic traumatology studies
n: In this lecture we shall consider forensic traumatology. The word traumatology comes from the Greek words trauma, that is, injury, and logos, that is, teaching, and means the science of injuries. In clinical medicine it mainly deals with the detection, treatment and prevention of injuries. Forensic traumatology determines the mechanism and time of infliction of an injury and the object that inflicted it. The forensic medical assessment of injuries and the resolution of other specific questions also occupy a main place.

t: The concept of bodily injury
n: Now the concept of bodily injury. In criminal law, bodily injury means harm caused to health by an intentional or negligent unlawful act. In forensic medicine, bodily injury is the disturbance of the anatomical integrity or physiological function of organs and tissues as a result of external action. Such a disturbance may lead to impairment of health or to death. Note that there is a risk of error here: an injury is not a disease. If the same condition arises from internal causes, it is understood as a disease.

t: Classification of damaging factors
n: Let us consider the classification of damaging factors. A damaging factor may be an object, a substance or a condition, that is, an event. Sometimes the combined action of several external factors is observed. According to the table, the factors are divided into four groups. Physical factors include mechanical, thermal, barometric, electrical and radiation action. Chemical factors are poisons, chemicals and drugs. Biological factors are toxins and pathogenic microbes. The mental factor includes strong emotion and fear. The consequences of mental action are usually studied by forensic psychiatry, and a forensic psychiatric examination is ordered.

t: Classification of injuries: simple, complex, combined, multiple
n: By the classification of injuries, simple, complex, combined and multiple injuries are distinguished. If an injury arose from the action of one factor, it is a simple injury; if from two or more kinds, a complex injury. An injury in one region or one segment is called limited; if in two or more regions or segments, a combined injury. By number, single and multiple injuries are distinguished. In the diagnosis these criteria must be determined first. Examples: a stab wound of the chest is simple, limited, single; rib fractures and a thermal burn are a complex, combined, multiple injury.

t: Anatomical and functional injuries
n: Let us look at anatomical and functional injuries. Anatomical structure and function are interrelated. In some injuries the morphological change is evident, in others the disturbance of function comes first. The predominantly anatomical group includes abrasions, bruises, wounds, fractures, dislocations, crush injuries and ruptures of internal organs. The predominantly functional group includes shock from a blow to a reflexogenic zone, concussion of the brain and internal organs, and aspiration asphyxia. Attention: this division is conditional, which is why it says "predominantly". Mechanical injuries are the leading ones in forensic examination; among causes of death they stand after cardiovascular and oncological diseases.

t: Case analysis: classifying an injury
n: Now a case analysis: classifying an injury. In case A there is a stab wound of the chest. In case B concussion of the brain and bruises in the abdominal region are observed. In case C there are rib fractures with a thermal burn added to them. Define each case by the classification criteria. The question is: what are the type of factor, the region and the number? The source gives the answer: case A is a simple, limited, single injury; case B is a simple, combined, multiple injury; case C is a complex, combined, multiple injury.

t: Traumatism and its kinds
n: Traumatism and its kinds. The totality of homogeneous injuries observed in persons under the same conditions of work and everyday life is called traumatism. Injuries most often occur because of failure to observe rules and from the consumption of alcohol and narcotics. By studying the factors, forensic examination materials make it possible to give concrete recommendations for prevention. Kinds of traumatism: occupational traumatism includes industrial, agricultural and construction. Transport traumatism includes car, motorcycle, bicycle, railway, air and water transport. Military traumatism is divided into wartime and peacetime. Others include street, sports, school and domestic traumatism.

t: Determining whether injuries were vital
n: Determining whether injuries were inflicted during life is of exceptional importance in forensic practice. The reason is that injuries may be inflicted after death too. This may be deliberate: dismemberment of the body or alteration of the original scene relating to the cause of death. It may also be accidental: during resuscitation, examination of the body or transportation, and also by animals, birds and fish. Vitality is determined by signs of the reaction of the whole organism or organ to the injury. Here, changes in the circulation are of main importance.

t: General and local signs of vitality
n: General and local signs of vitality. General signs reflect the reaction of the whole organism, local signs the change in the region of the injury. General signs include external and internal bleeding, anaemia, aspiration of blood into the airways, myoglobin, erythrophagocytosis, and air, fat and tissue embolism. Local signs include haemorrhage into the region of the injury, thrombus in vessels, reactive oedema, inflammation, necrosis and muscle contraction. The clarity of the signs depends on the kind, number and extent of the injury and on the characteristics of the organism and region. Attention: in some phylogenetically older tissues a postmortem injury may look vital.

t: Methods of examining injuries
n: Methods of examining injuries. An injury is first examined macroscopically: the kind, location, shape, colour, ends of the wound, edges, floor and wall are assessed. Stereomicroscopy is used for spatial study, and the trace-evidence method to identify the damaging object. If necessary, forensic biological, forensic chemical and histochemical laboratory methods are also used. The table gives the methods and their tasks. Measurement determines the size of the injury and the distance from a body landmark. Radiography shows a foreign body and bone injury. Colour print and spectral analysis find metal particles and traces. Histological examination determines vitality and the age of infliction.

t: Quick question and case analysis: vitality, medical document
n: Quick question: which signs confirm vitality? General signs: bleeding, aspiration, embolism. Local signs: haemorrhage, thrombus, reactive oedema. Now a case: an injury was found on a body. The expert checks for haemorrhage, oedema, inflammation, necrosis and thrombus; they indicate a vital injury. Attention: the clarity of signs depends on the kind, number and extent of the injury; in phylogenetically ancient tissues a postmortem injury may resemble a vital one. One more important point: if the description in a clinician's document is incomplete or only a diagnosis is written, carrying out the tasks of the examination becomes seriously difficult.

t: Mechanical injuries and injuring agents
n: Mechanical injuries and injuring agents. Movement is necessary for a mechanical injury; its extent is directly proportional to the mass of the object or body and to velocity. Mechanical injuries are divided into those inflicted by blunt objects, sharp objects and firearms. The extent is also affected by the mass of the object, hardness, velocity, the characteristics of the injured region, age and diseases. Agents are divided into three groups. A weapon is specially made for attack or defence, for example a pistol. An implement is used in the home or in industry, for example an axe or a saw. An object is a thing with no definite purpose, for example a stone or a stick.

t: Causes of death from mechanical injury: general scheme
n: The general scheme of causes of death from mechanical injury. The causes are divided into primary and secondary. In primary causes, death occurs a short time after the injury. In secondary causes, death occurs after some interval. Primary causes include an injury incompatible with life, for example decapitation, and injury to vital organs, for example cardiac contusion. Secondary causes include infectious complications, traumatic toxicosis, secondary blood loss, shock and embolism. In particular, sepsis, gas gangrene and tetanus are secondary causes.

t: Secondary causes: infection and intoxication
n: Secondary causes: infection and intoxication. Secondary causes include various infectious complications: purulent peritonitis, pleurisy, meningitis and osteomyelitis leading to sepsis. Anaerobic infection, that is, gas gangrene and tetanus, and also intoxication, that is, traumatic toxicosis, are likewise considered secondary causes. Sometimes, after an injury, secondary blood loss, shock and embolism are observed. In addition, a malignant tumour may develop in the area of injury. That is, secondary causes fall into four groups: infectious complications, anaerobic infection, intoxication and other complications.

t: Blood loss: acute and massive
n: Blood loss: acute and massive. In injury to a large artery, even with loss of up to 500 ml of blood, death occurs within minutes from ventricular fibrillation. Minakov's spots are band-like haemorrhages under the endocardium of the left ventricle, characteristic of acute blood loss. If more than 50% of the blood is lost, that is, 2.5 l or more, death occurs more slowly, over several hours. In acute loss, only the brain and heart are anaemic, the spleen is firm, and the cadaveric lividity is as usual. In massive loss there is general anaemia, the spleen is shrunken, cadaveric lividity is late and scanty, and Minakov's spots are found only in some cases.

t: Traumatic shock and compression of organs
n: Traumatic shock and compression of organs. Traumatic shock is the organism's response to injury with serious disturbance of the activity of the central nervous, cardiovascular and endocrine systems. In shock, peripheral circulation is inadequate: a disproportion arises between the amount of circulating blood and the volume of the vascular system. Severe grade III–IV shock usually leads to death; venous congestion, pooling of blood and disturbance of microcirculation are found. The brain and spinal cord, heart and lungs are compressed by blood and air: in intracranial haematomas, haemopericardium, pneumothorax and haemothorax.

t: Embolism: air and fat; aspiration of blood
n: Embolism: air and fat, and also aspiration of blood. 5–7 cubic centimetres of air dissolve; if 10 cubic centimetres or more enter a vein rapidly, death is possible. Fat embolism occurs in fractures of long bones; death occurs on days 2–3 and is confirmed by staining with Sudan III/IV. In injury of the larynx and fractures of the skull base and nasal bones, aspiration of blood leads to asphyxia. To detect air embolism, the Suntsov test is used. In the first stage, the chest is opened and the sternum is separated. Then an incision is made in the front part of the pericardial sac and water is poured in. Then the wall of the right ventricle is pierced with the tip of a scalpel. If air bubbles come out of the water, the result is positive.

t: Case analysis and quick question: mechanical causes of death
n: Case analysis and quick question: mechanical causes of death. Situation: 2–3 days after a fracture of a long tubular bone, the victim died. Question: what is the cause of death? Answer: fat embolism. Small particles of fat collect in the pulmonary vessels and gradually block their lumen, which is why death is delayed. For confirmation, frozen sections of the lungs and brain are stained with Sudan III, that is, orange-red, or Sudan IV, that is, black. Attention: air embolism is not fat embolism. For air the Suntsov test is used; for fat, Sudan staining and a delay of 2–3 days are characteristic.

t: Blood loss and embolism: important figures
n: Important figures on blood loss and embolism. In injury to a large artery, even with loss of up to 500 ml of blood, death may occur in the first minutes from ventricular fibrillation. Massive blood loss is more than 50%, that is, 2.5 litres or more; with it, death occurs over several hours. In air embolism, 5–7 cubic centimetres of air dissolve in the blood, while the rapid entry of 10 cubic centimetres or more may lead to death. In fat embolism, death occurs 2–3 days after the injury. Remember: these figures are given in the source Giyasov, pp. 31–32.

t: Blunt objects: kinds and surface of action
n: Blunt objects: kinds and surface of action. Hard objects are distinguished, for example a stone and a stick; soft objects, for example a scarf and a towel; and elastic objects, for example a rubber ball. A direct injury arises at the site of action, an indirect injury in a region other than the site of action. Limited and unlimited surface are relative concepts: the surface of the object is assessed in comparison with the area of injury. If the surface of the object is smaller than the surface of the region, it is called limited; if larger, it is considered broad. If the mass of the object is smaller than the mass of the region, impression trauma results. If the force of action is much greater than the mass of the region, inertial trauma is produced.

t: Impression and inertial trauma
n: Impression and inertial trauma. If the mass of the damaging object is smaller than the mass of the injured region of the body, impression trauma arises. In impression trauma the injury is confined to the area of action alone. If the force of action is much greater than the mass of the region or body, inertial trauma, that is, acceleration trauma, develops. In inertial trauma, indirect injuries, signs of general concussion of the body and, in craniocerebral injuries, contrecoup are found. In brief: in impression trauma the injury is only at the site of action, whereas in inertial trauma indirect injuries, general concussion and contrecoup are observed.

t: Mechanisms of action of blunt objects
n: Mechanisms of action of blunt objects. In torsion, two rotational forces act in opposite directions; a spiral fracture forms in the bone. In concussion, a weak action causes concussion of the brain, a strong one injury to internal organs and ligaments. In most cases an injury is formed through two or more mechanisms. A blow is a brief action in one direction and gives an abrasion, a bruise and a contused wound. Compression is a centripetal, prolonged action and makes injury to internal organs and bones more severe. Tension gives a lacerated wound, rupture and avulsion. Friction is movement at an angle to the body and forms only direct injuries, mainly abrasions.

t: Abrasion and its stages
n: Abrasion and its stages. If only the epidermis is damaged, it is a superficial abrasion; if it reaches the papillary layer, it is called a deep abrasion. A linear abrasion is called a scratch. If the angle of action is acute, the shape is arc-like. The time periods are conditional; they depend on age, skin and depth, for example the crust persists for 4–6 hours, while the trace persists for 30+ days. The stages are as follows. A fresh abrasion, up to 12 hours, has a moist surface, then dries. A crust forms up to 2–3 days. Epithelialisation continues up to 7–9 days, and the crust begins to come away. The trace, in the form of a pink spot, disappears on days 10–15.

t: Forensic medical significance of abrasion
n: The forensic medical significance of abrasion. Firstly, an abrasion confirms that there was mechanical action. Secondly, the mechanism and age of the injury can be determined from an abrasion. Thirdly, from the location, shape and number, the circumstances of the incident can be inferred. For example, an arc-shaped abrasion on the neck may point to manual strangulation. Fourthly, the severity of bodily injuries is sometimes determined from abrasions. That is, although an abrasion looks simple, it serves the expert as an important source of information.

t: Bruise and colour change
n: Bruise and colour change. A bruise is haemorrhage into soft tissue when a blood vessel ruptures; if blood collects in a cavity, it is called a haematoma. From an object with a limited surface, the shape of the bruise resembles the object; with an unlimited one, it is round or oval. An indirect bruise appears later, and the colour is also delayed; the shape does not depend on the surface of the object. Colour dynamics: in the first days reddish-bluish or bluish because of reduction of oxyhaemoglobin. On days 3–4 green, because of verdohaemochromogen and biliverdin. On days 6–8 yellow, because of bilirubin and haemosiderin. On the eyes, lips and neck, a bruise does not change hue but slowly fades.

t: Wounds and ruptures from a blunt object
n: Wounds and ruptures from a blunt object. A contused wound is produced by a blow and compression; a crushed wound by a stronger blow and compression; a lacerated wound by a blow and tension. A flap wound arises from a blow and tension at an acute angle. The shape of the wound corresponds to the shape of the surface. Attention: a wound is not a rupture! A rupture is always an indirect injury, formed by tension near a bony prominence. Differences: the ends of a wound are usually blunt, whereas the ends of a rupture are often sharp. The edges of a wound are uneven and abraded; the edges of a rupture are even, without abrasion. On the marginal wall of a wound there are tissue bridges; in a rupture the wall is vertical.

t: Bone fractures: kinds and deformation
n: Bone fractures: kinds and deformation. In temporary deformation, the bone regains its shape after the action ends; in permanent deformation, a fracture occurs. In a complete fracture the fragments are displaced in several directions; in an incomplete one, movement is in only one direction. In life a fracture determines the degree of severity; after death, over time, it helps to determine the mechanism and the instrument. Classification of fractures: by the condition of the skin, open and closed; in an open fracture the bone is in communication with the external environment. The fracture line may be transverse, longitudinal, diagonal or spiral. The form may be linear, comminuted, depressed and other.

t: Signs of the tension and compression sides in bending
n: Signs of the tension and compression sides in bending. In bending, two forces act on the bone at an angle; on the side of action there is compression, on the opposite side tension. Bone is less resistant to tension, so a fracture appears first on the tension side, then on the compression side. Bending is the most frequent kind of permanent deformation; the side of the force is determined by the difference in signs. On the tension side the fracture line is a single straight line, mainly transverse, the surface is perpendicular to the bone, the edges are even or finely serrated, and there are no fragments. On the compression side there are one or two lines, zigzag, the surface is at an angle to the bone, and the edges are uneven and coarsely serrated.

t: Rib fracture, dislocations, resuscitation fracture
n: Rib fracture, dislocations and resuscitation fracture. In compression, two forces act on the bone towards each other; in torsion a spiral fracture forms. Tension is very rare. In indirect cardiac massage the sternum breaks directly and the ribs indirectly. This artificial fracture must be distinguished from a fracture produced by a blow. In a direct fracture there is a sign of compression on the outer plate and of tension on the inner plate. In an indirect fracture it is the reverse, and there is usually no external injury. A dislocation is always an indirect injury: the articular surfaces are persistently displaced, and external injury is not characteristic. Fractures are detected by X-ray and CT.

t: Case analysis: a complex of blunt injuries
n: Case analysis: a complex of blunt injuries. Situation: the ribs are broken in the body of a person who underwent resuscitation. Question: is this a fracture from a blow or from cardiac massage? Path to a solution: in the area of the fracture, look at the signs of compression and tension on the outer and inner plates, and at the presence of external injury. Attention: an abrasion is not a parchment-like spot. A parchment-like spot is yellow-brown, forms no crust, and has none of the changes characteristic of a vital injury. Further attention: a bruise is not a cadaveric lividity patch. In regions where cadaveric lividity is located, deciding whether a bruise is present is harder.

t: Injuries from falls: kinds and stages
n: Injuries from falls: kinds and stages. In forensic medicine, a fall from a height and a fall on the level, that is, from one's own height, are distinguished. A fall from a height may be direct, stepwise or non-free; and also passive, that is, accidental, and active, that is, with a push or a jump. The stages: in stage I balance is lost; in stage II there is movement around the centre of gravity; in stage III–IV, separation and flight; in stage V, impact on the surface; in stage VI, inertia and a secondary blow. Most of the principal injuries form at stage V, when the body strikes the surface.

t: Fall from a height: landing position and injuries
n: Fall from a height: landing position and injuries. A direct injury forms on the part that landed on the surface, an indirect injury in other regions. A secondary injury occurs on the side to which the body's movement was directed; in a fall onto the body it is not characteristic. A characteristic sign: external injury mainly on one side, while internal injuries are wider and more serious. In a fall onto the head, direct multifragmentary skull fractures and brain damage are seen, and indirect fractures of the cervical vertebrae and ribs. In a fall onto the feet, fractures of the heel and ankle and contused wounds are direct, and fractures of the femoral neck, pelvis and spine are indirect injuries. Cases of landing on the knees and buttocks are also given in the table.

t: Comparison of a fall on the level and a fall from a height
n: Let us compare a fall on the level and a fall from a height. A fall on the level has 3 stages: balance is lost, the body begins to fall and strikes the surface. In a blow to the back or side, brain injury is strong in the region of contrecoup; in a fall onto the face there is no contrecoup. A fall from a height, by contrast, has six stages, a secondary injury is possible, and injuries of the internal organs are serious. In a fall on the level there is no secondary injury, and contusion and concussion are not characteristic. Remember: clothing and footwear must be taken undamaged and quickly handed over to law enforcement authorities.

t: Sharp objects: general description and cutting objects
n: Sharp objects: general description and cutting objects. If the radius of the arc formed by the edges is 0.1 mm or less, it is a sharp blade or point. A sharp object always produces a direct injury. Unlike a blunt object, here the separation of tissues is primary and crushing secondary. The object may be cutting, piercing, chopping, sawing or combined. Traces of the injury remain on clothing: it must be removed carefully, dried at room temperature, wrapped in paper and handed to the investigator. An incised wound is spindle-shaped, the edges are even and not abraded, and the ends are sharp; at the end there may be a "swallowtail". The length is greater than the depth.

t: Injuries from piercing objects
n: Injuries from piercing objects. The shape of the wound depends on the cross-section of the object: with an oval or round cross-section the wound is oval, slit-like, with even edges. If the cross-section is greater than 5 mm, the rim is clearly visible: with perpendicular action it is circular, with oblique action segmental. The external dimension is smaller than the depth; the object may pierce cartilage and flat bone, and internal bleeding may be heavy. The difference between entrance and exit holes: the size of the entrance is slightly smaller than the cross-section of the object, there may be an abrasion rim along the edges, and contamination may be detected. The exit hole is larger than the entrance, the rim is absent or smaller, and contamination with foreign matter is not observed.

t: Injuries from piercing-cutting objects
n: Injuries from piercing-cutting objects. A blade has both a sharp point and a sharp edge: the point enters the tissue, and the edge cuts it apart. If the blade acts perpendicularly, the wound is smaller; if the angle of action is acute, a wound of larger size is produced. The wound track usually corresponds to the length of the blade; in a soft area under strong pressure it may be longer than the blade. Depending on the kind of blade, the shape of the wound differs. With a double-edged dagger, the wound is spindle-shaped, oval, with even edges and both ends sharp. With a single-edged knife, the wound is elongated wedge-shaped, P-shaped, with one end sharp and the other blunt.

t: Injuries from chopping and sawing objects
n: Injuries from chopping and sawing objects. Chopping objects, that is, an axe, an adze, a sickle and a spade, have a sharp edge and a large mass; on impact the edge cuts the tissue and the sides push it aside. Chop wounds are extensive, are more often found on the head and arms, and bone and brain are also damaged. They are more often accidental, very rarely homicidal. With perpendicular action the wound is slit-like with even edges; on the cranial vault, perpendicular action gives a slit-like fracture and oblique action a comminuted fracture. Sawing objects are rare: accidents occur in the home and in the woodworking industry. The teeth of a saw are triangular, set outward to the sides.

t: Chop wounds according to direction of the blade
n: Chop wounds differ according to the direction of the blade. When the sharp edge of the chopping part acts perpendicularly, slit-like, oval wounds with even edges are produced; if the edge is blunter, the edges are finely serrated. When a chopping object acts obliquely on the body, an arc-shaped wound is produced, and on the side of the acute angle, signs of abrasion and crushing appear at the edges. When the chopping object penetrates fully, the ends of the wound are blunt, with additional cracks; on the marginal walls there are signs of crushing and comminution. If the object penetrates partially, the end corresponding to the sharp edge is sharp, and the end corresponding to the more deeply entered part is blunt.

t: Wounds from sawing objects
n: Wounds from sawing objects. Saws are of elongated blade, circular, wire and other forms, with many sharp triangular teeth. The teeth of a saw are set out to the sides, that is, splayed, so the kerf is wider than the thickness of the saw blade. With a blade saw, the wound is linear, the edges are finely serrated and uneven; at the ends there is a superficial cut and a scratch, and on the saw-cut surface of bone parallel ridges and grooves are seen. With a circular saw, the edges of the wound are uneven, serrated and finely flapped; the saw-cut surfaces of bones are relatively even, with arc-shaped marks.

t: Case analysis: sharp objects and final conclusion
n: Case analysis: sharp objects and final conclusion. Situation: a knife wound in the chest region has penetrated into the cavity. Question: is this a stab wound or a stab-incised wound? Attention: a stab wound is not a stab-incised wound. A piercing object pushes the tissue aside, whereas a piercing-cutting object cuts it apart with its sharp edge. The entrance wound and the wound track are distinguished. The length of the track usually corresponds to the length of the blade, and under strong pressure may be longer than the blade. Conclusion: the clothing must be removed carefully, dried at room temperature, placed in a paper package and handed to the investigator.
